common_name: Small Leaf Tea Camellia (Compact China-Type Tea Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this China-type selection is prized for its small, delicate leaves rather than any single named breeding program, making it a widely propagated seedling strain among specialty tea nurseries.

directions: Small Leaf is a classic small-leaved China-type (var. sinensis) tea selection, propagated by specialty camellia nurseries from a long-cultivated Southeastern stock plant, and grown for its compact, container-friendly, densely branching habit. Leaves stay under about 4 inches long, giving a fine-textured hedge and a milder, more delicate cup than larger-leaved types. Provide morning sun with afternoon shade, keep the soil consistently moist and acidic, and expect a rounded shrub reaching roughly 3 to 6 feet in a decade. Begin light plucking of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old.

common_name: Large Leaf Tea Camellia (Tetraploid White Tea Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this tetraploid selection, originally introduced by the USDA in the 1970s, grows as a large, tree-form shrub rather than the more compact form typical of China-type tea.

directions: Large Leaf is a tetraploid tea selection, originally distributed through a 1970s USDA introduction, distinguished by thick, leathery, strongly veined leaves up to 6 inches long and unusually large buds and flowers. Its natural tendency is to grow as a multi-trunked small tree rather than a rounded shrub, eventually reaching 10 feet or more, so give it more room than a typical China-type tea plant. The oversized buds make it a favorite among home tea growers specifically for white tea production. Keep soil consistently moist and acidic, and expect somewhat variable seed set, a known trait of tetraploid Camellia selections.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service Tea Research

common_name: Black Sea Tea (Georgian Coastal Cold-Hardy Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Black Sea Tea descends from tea research stock grown along the Black Sea coast of the country of Georgia, sharing much of its cold-hardy heritage with the related Sochi selection.

directions: Black Sea Tea traces to former Soviet-era tea research plantings on the Georgian coast of the Black Sea, a growing region with a climate more similar to the American mid-South than to tea's native subtropical range. Like its close relative Sochi, it was selected primarily for cold tolerance and vigorous, reliable growth rather than for any single specialized tea style, producing narrow, roughly 4 to 5 inch leaves on a broad, multi-stemmed shrub. Home growers value it for pushing tea cultivation into cooler zones than typical China-type selections tolerate. Provide the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and partial shade recommended for other tea camellias, and begin harvesting once plants are three to four years old.

common_name: Fairhope Select Tea (Gulf Coast Alabama Heritage Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Fairhope Select descends from surviving plants of a Lipton-sponsored tea research planting in Fairhope, Alabama, later rescued and propagated by grower Donnie Barrett.

directions: Fairhope Select is a Gulf Coast heirloom tea selection with a direct link to Lipton's mid-20th-century Fairhope, Alabama tea research plantation; when that project was abandoned, a handful of surviving plants were rescued and propagated into the selections sold today. It carries small to medium, heavily serrated green leaves, tolerates more direct sun than many China-type tea plants, and flowers and sets seed prolifically. Vigorous shoot production makes it a productive choice for growers wanting green or black tea from the same plant. Give it the standard acidic, well-drained, evenly moist soil tea camellias require, and expect solid performance across the humid Gulf South.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dave's Fave was selected from Chinese seedling stock of unknown provenance for its rounded, glossy, dark-green leaves and short internodes, giving it an especially dense, hedge-friendly form.

directions: Dave's Fave was selected by a camellia nursery breeder for its exceptionally dark, glossy, rounded leaves and short spacing between leaf nodes, producing a naturally dense, well-shaped shrub that needs little corrective pruning to serve as a tea hedge. Its sturdy, woody stems hold up well under repeated harvesting. Trial processing has shown it yields a cup broadly comparable to the cold-hardy Sochi selection, though it was chosen for form rather than winter hardiness specifically. Grow it in the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade recommended for other China-type tea camellias, and begin light plucking once plants are established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Teabreeze was selected from commercial tea stock primarily for its ornamental, fountain-shaped growth habit and highly glossy, narrow foliage.

directions: Teabreeze stands out among tea camellias for its arching, fountain-like growth habit, eventually reaching 8 to 15 feet, with narrow, deeply lacquered dark-green leaves up to 4 inches long. Lightly fragrant white flowers appear in fall against the glossy foliage, giving it strong ornamental appeal alongside its usefulness for green tea production. Because of its ultimate size, give it more room than a typical compact China-type selection, and site it where its graceful form can be appreciated as a specimen or informal screen. Maintain the same acidic, evenly moist soil and partial shade other tea camellias require.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Miwa is notable for its contrasting red-brown young stems set against exceptionally narrow, dark-green leaves.

directions: Miwa is an ornamental tea selection best recognized by its reddish-brown new stems, which contrast strikingly with narrow, dark-green leaves only about an inch wide. It grows into a rounded shrub roughly 6 feet tall and wide over a decade, making it a manageable size for home tea gardens. The fine-textured foliage suits it to both landscape use and light tea production. Provide consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and begin harvesting the top two leaves and a bud once the plant is well established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Yellow Tea is distinguished from other named tea selections by its unusually large leaves that are heavily splotched with yellow variegation.

directions: Yellow Tea is grown chiefly as an ornamental tea camellia, valued for leaves that can reach nearly 8 inches long and are heavily marked with yellow variegation, a striking departure from the uniform dark green of most tea selections. The oversized foliage also gives it novelty appeal for home tea processing, though the name refers to its leaf color rather than to Chinese "yellow tea" processing methods. Grow it as you would any China-type tea camellia, in evenly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with some afternoon shade to protect the variegated leaves from scorch. Expect a full-sized shrub similar in stature to standard tea camellias.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Super Sochi was cloned from vigorous, large-leaved individuals within the original Sochi cold-hardy tea population and named for combining superior leaf size with Sochi's Black Sea cold tolerance.

directions: Super Sochi was selected from within the classic cold-hardy Sochi tea population for individuals with noticeably larger leaves and more vigorous growth, while retaining Sochi's Black Sea coastal heritage and cold tolerance. It suits growers who want to push tea cultivation into the cooler end of zone 6 while still harvesting enough leaf for meaningful batches of green, oolong, or black tea. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil and partial shade other tea camellias need, with good winter mulch in its coldest growing zones. Expect a broad, multi-stemmed shrub reaching roughly 8 feet in a decade under good conditions.

common_name: Chia Tsao Tea (Taiwan Mountain Oolong Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chia Tsao was collected from tea gardens at the mountain village of the same name in Taiwan and is prized specifically for producing highly aromatic oolong tea.

directions: Chia Tsao originates from tea gardens in the mountain village of the same name in Taiwan, and is grown chiefly for the unusually fragrant oolong tea its small, narrow leaves produce when processed with partial oxidation. The plant has a more open, spreading habit than typical China-type tea camellias, rather than the dense upright form of many named selections. Growers have reported it tolerating brief drops into the mid-20s Fahrenheit without injury, suggesting reasonable cold tolerance for the humid Southeast. Provide the standard acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade recommended for other tea camellias, and process the harvested flush as oolong to showcase its signature aroma.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Silver Dust is a slow-growing, compact variegated selection whose new spring flush emerges nearly pure white before shifting to light green and, eventually, standard green.

directions: Silver Dust is grown primarily as an ornamental tea camellia for containers or small garden beds, valued for white speckling across its leaf surface and for a first spring flush that can emerge nearly pure white before greening with age, as is typical of leaf variegation. Its slow growth rate and naturally mounded form keep it compact and tidy without much pruning. A small test batch of tea made from the white shoots has been described as very mild with little bitterness, though it is chosen mainly for foliage interest rather than yield. Grow it in the same acidic, evenly moist soil and partial shade other tea camellias require.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Rosea corresponds to the botanical form Camellia sinensis var. sinensis forma rosea, first described by Japanese botanists, and was introduced into the US nursery trade through the South Carolina Botanical Garden and the federal Bureau of Plant Introductions.

directions: Rosea is grown chiefly as an ornamental tea camellia, notable for pale pink autumn flowers with bright pink filaments and for red pigment that runs through the whole plant, from roots to new burgundy-tinted growth. Its tiny, dark, smooth-textured leaves and slow growth rate make it well suited to containers or a fine-textured tea hedge for patient gardeners. It corresponds to a botanical form first described in Japan and later introduced to American cultivation through South Carolina plant-introduction channels. Provide the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade recommended for other tea camellias.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Brew-Tea-Ful was selected for its naturally compact, densely branching form, which needs little pruning and suits container culture better than leggier tea selections.

directions: Brew-Tea-Ful is a compact tea camellia bred specifically for container growing, with a naturally dense, well-branched form that requires minimal shaping compared to more open, leggy tea selections. It produces respectable green or black tea from the same harvested flush, making it a practical option for patio or small-space tea gardens rather than field-scale production. Keep it in a large container of acidic, well-drained potting mix, water consistently, and site it in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once the plant is well established.
